description: Interfaces and type aliases — describing the shape of your data.

screens.body:
Most bugs aren't about single values — they're about objects with the wrong shape. A user object missing its email, a config without its port. The function runs fine until it reaches for a property that isn't there.

Interfaces describe the shape of an object: which properties it has and what types they are. Define the shape once, and TypeScript checks every object against it.

options: The shape of an object: its properties and their types
check.question: What does an interface describe?

screens.heading: Shapes, not just values
screens.keyPoint: Interfaces describe object shapes; TS checks every object.

screens.body:
The syntax: the keyword interface, a name in PascalCase, and the properties in curly braces. Each property gets name: type.

Then you use it as a type annotation — on variables, function parameters, return values. Anywhere a type can go, an interface can go.
screens.heading: Writing an interface
screens.keyPoint: interface Name { prop: type } — then use Name as a type.

screens.body:
Not every property is required. A ? marks a property as optional — the object is valid with or without it.

This is perfect for real-world data: a user might not have set their bio yet, a product might not have a discount. Optional properties model reality instead of pretending every field is always there.

check.question: How do you mark a property optional in an interface?

screens.heading: Optional properties
screens.keyPoint: prop?: type — valid with or without the property.

screens.body:
A type alias gives a name to any type — not just objects. type ID = string means "wherever you see ID, it's really a string."

Aliases shine for unions: string | number means "either a string or a number." Status fields, IDs that can be two shapes, function signatures — aliases name them so your code reads like English.

options: A name for any type, including unions
A type that can never be used
check.question: What is a type alias?

screens.heading: Type aliases: names for types
screens.keyPoint: type X = ... names any type — great for unions.

screens.body:
Interfaces and type aliases overlap, so here's the simple rule: use interface for object shapes (especially ones you'll extend or implement), use type for unions, tuples, and function signatures.

You'll see both in the wild. Being able to read both matters more than picking perfectly.

options: Interfaces for object shapes, types for unions
check.question: The practical rule for interface vs type:

screens.heading: Interface vs type: the simple rule
screens.keyPoint: interface for shapes, type for unions and signatures.

screens.body:
Interfaces can extend each other: an Admin is a User plus extra fields. You write only the new parts.

And readonly marks a property as set-once — TypeScript stops anyone from reassigning it later. IDs, creation dates, config loaded at startup: if it shouldn't change, say so.

options: interface Admin extends User { role: string }
check.question: How does Admin inherit all of User's fields?

screens.heading: Extending and readonly
screens.keyPoint: extends inherits shapes; readonly locks a property.

screens.body:
Nested objects get nested interfaces — just describe each level. And arrays of objects are Type[] — "an array where every item matches this shape."

This is exactly what API responses look like: an array of shaped objects. Type the response once, and every .map and .filter over it is checked.

check.question: The type for an array of User objects:

screens.heading: Nesting shapes
screens.keyPoint: Interfaces nest; Comment[] = array of that shape.
